samples.text:
The table shows the percentage of people who had access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation in five regions of the world in 2000 and 2020.

In general, access to water was better than access to sanitation in all regions, and both of them improved between 2000 and 2020.

Firstly, for drinking water, Europe had the highest percentage in both years, 98% and 99%. Latin America was also high with 88% in 2000 and 96% in 2020. East Asia and South Asia was similar, they increased from 82% to 94% and from 80% to 92%. Sub-Saharan Africa was the lowest, only 46% in 2000, but it rose to 65% in 2020.

Secondly, the sanitation figures was lower. Europe had 92% and then 95%, and Latin America had 70% and 87%. In East Asia it improve from 55% to 83%. South Asia had a big increase, from 22% to 60%, it is the biggest change in the table. Sub-Saharan Africa had 23% in 2000 and 33% in 2020, so it was still the lowest in the end.
samples.why: Relevant overview and accurate data · both services covered but details listed region by region with little comparison · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly) · agreement errors and comma splices that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The table compares the proportion of people in five regions of the world who had access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, access to both services improved in every region over the twenty years, although safe water was consistently more widely available than sanitation. Europe had the highest levels of provision, whereas Sub-Saharan Africa lagged far behind the other regions.

As regards drinking water, nearly all Europeans had access, with the figure rising from 98% to 99%. Latin America, East Asia and South Asia also had high levels, ranging from 80% to 88% in 2000 and increasing to between 92% and 96% in 2020. By contrast, fewer than half of the population of Sub-Saharan Africa had safe water in 2000 (46%), although this improved to 65% by 2020.

Sanitation showed more significant differences. In Europe the figure was 92% in 2000 and 95% in 2020, while Latin America rose from 70% to 87%. The most dramatic improvements occurred in Asia: East Asia's rate went up from 55% to 83%, and South Asia's almost tripled from 22% to 60%. Sub-Saharan Africa, however, only rose by ten points to 33%, meaning two thirds of people still lacked basic sanitation.
samples.why: Clear overview with the leading and lagging regions identified · data grouped effectively into ranges · good cohesion and collocation (lagged behind, provision) · frequent error-free sentences with minor awkwardness.

samples.text:
The table shows the percentage of the population in five world regions with access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation in 2000 and 2020.

It is evident that provision of both services expanded everywhere over the two decades, but access to sanitation remained lower than access to safe water in every region. Europe enjoyed near-universal coverage throughout, while Sub-Saharan Africa trailed well behind on both measures.

Safe water was already widely available in most regions in 2000, ranging from 80% in South Asia to 98% in Europe. By 2020, these four regions had all reached 92% or more, with Europe at 99%. Sub-Saharan Africa was the clear outlier: less than half its population (46%) had safe water at the start of the period, and although this rose by 19 percentage points, about a third of people still lacked access in 2020.

The gaps in sanitation were far wider. South Asia made the most striking progress, its coverage soaring from 22% to 60%, while East Asia also recorded a substantial rise of 28 points, reaching 83%. Latin America improved from 70% to 87%, and Europe from an already high 92% to 95%. In Sub-Saharan Africa, however, the figure increased only modestly, from 23% to 33%, leaving it the lowest in the table.
samples.why: Precise overview · key contrasts selected skilfully with accurate derived differences · seamless cohesion and paragraphing · wide, natural vocabulary (outlier, near-universal coverage) · varied, accurate complex structures.
